Issued at 216 PM CDT Tue Oct 27 2026

Tonight: Scattered Light Showers Continue

A weak warm frontal boundary is lifting north across the area 
helping to induce some light showers across the Upper Mississippi 
Valley this afternoon. These transient showers are producing little 
in the way of QPF with only a couple hundreths being reported at 
most in any given location. These will continue to lift to the north 
along with the front. In addition, a weak stationary boundary and 
axis of 850 mb moisture transport into our area is providing a 
steady fetch of light showers over Northeast Iowa and Southeast 
Minnesota this afternoon. This is noted on RAP 27.18 mesoanalysis 
with a small axis of 1+ pWats and across our area coinciding with a 
modestly strong 850 moisture transport vector. Even with this better 
fetch of moisture, still not expecting more than 0.05 inches of 
additional precipitation at any location. Overnight lows tonight 
will be on the warmer side compared to previous nights (upper 40s to 
low 50s) thanks to prolonged cloud cover and southerly return flow 
increasing low level moisture across the region. 

Wednesday - Thursday: Potential Record Warmth, Rain/Storms 

A low amplitude trough axis is expected to eject out of the 
Intermountain West and into the North Central Rockies/Plains through 
the day on Wednesday with strong southwesterly flow out ahead of it. 
At the surface, a family of weak lows, one across the southern 
Canadian Plains and one across the Northern Great Plains will start 
to move northeast, connected in part by a cold front. The low to the 
north is expected to become the more dominant low of the two with 
more support in the left exit region of the upper level jet. This 
setup overall: the two surface lows, the trailing cold front, the 
strong upper jet ahead of a upper trough axis all look to provide 
favorable synoptic kinematics across the region. In addition, 
moisture is expected to continue to pool ahead of the front with 
strong return flow through the day and near 60 deg dew points and 
surface temps in the low to mid 70s. This is a relatively
anomalous setup for late October and has allowed for the chance
to see some thunderstorms tomorrow afternoon/evening (a few 
strong storms possible) primarily across Southeast Minnesota. 
The thermodynamic parameter space does not look very favorable 
with weak mid level lapse rates below 7 deg C/km and elevated 
MLCAPE between 500-1000 J/kg. However, given the favorable 
kinematic space with 35-45 kts of effective bulk shear expected 
and low level curvature in the hodographs leading to increased 
SRH, this does give pause to the possibility supercells of all 
hazards being possible. Cloud cover and MLCIN will be of 
significant hindrance but if storms can become surface based 
along the front (potentially near the I-35 corridor?) some 
strong to severe storms may be possible. There is still 
significant uncertainty given this potential with only a 5% 
chance of severe weather in the Day 2 SPC Convective Outlook. 
Better chances overall look to be to our west across South 
Central Minnesota as the frontal boundary doesn't make it to our
doorstep likely until after peak heating. This potential will 
be monitored closely over the next 24 hours. 

After the front moves through overnight into THursday, rain chances 
are expected to come to an end with dry conditions expected during 
the day on Thursday. High temperatures will go back down much closer 
to normal in the upper 50s to mid 60s. 

Friday - Early Next Week: Continued Rain Chances 

A low confidence forecast continues for this weekend with chances 
for rain returning Friday and continuing off and on through the 
weekend and into early next week. This is due in large part to an 
upper trough moving northeast out of the Desert Southwest (cutoff 
from the main jet over the Pac NW). As this moves northeast, this 
will help send another surge of moisture northward into the Mid and 
Upper Mississippi River Valleys. There are ensemble differences as 
to how this cutoff trough is handled through the weekend but the 
general consensus is that it will provide some kind of upper support 
to allow for additional rainfall across the area. Finer details will 
be sorted out in the coming days as the trough evolution will 
determine local impacts. 

Looking just beyond the scope of this forecast, both EC and GFS 
ensemble members are locking onto a relatively strong cut off low 
forming by early/mid next week across the Central Rockies. How this 
cutoff low evolves could play a significant impact across the area 
with the EC solutions favoring a more northward swing, bringing 
additional bouts of heavy rain across the area. There is still much 
that can change with this but it bares watching over the coming 
days.
